me.challenges: This section lists all the challenges you've received and issued.
me.completed: Once you've finished a game, you'll find it here. Games automatically drop off this list 48 hours after you last visited it. You can manually remove a game from this list by clicking the Clear button. If someone comments on a completed game, it will reappear on this list and will be bolded.
me.issueChallenge: This is how you issue challenges for all the various games. You can also issue challenges from the list of games or from any of the other list pages (like the ratings page).
me.settings: And finally, open your user settings to change your profile, notification preferences, and exploration settings. You can disable these tours there as well.
me.theirturn: If it's your opponent's turn in any games, they'll be listed here. You can sort this table too.

play.board: This is the heart and soul of any game: the board. Click on the board to make your move. Helpful hints will appear above the move entry box as you do so.
play.boardbuttons: Below the board is a series of buttons that let you do things like rotate the board and take notes. The gear icon opens board display settings and lets you turn last-move annotations off and on. The paint-brush icon opens per-game visual customization. None of these buttons will harm your game, so click around and explore!
play.chat: The best part about playing games is the people you play with. This is where you can talk back and forth with your opponent. The user chats are gathered here for your convenience, but a list of *all* chats, including textual descriptions of what's happening in the game, is visible at the bottom of the screen. Remember that these chats are public. Please see our terms of service and privacy policy for details.
play.move: This is where you enter your move. Most of the time, you can make your move simply by clicking on the board, but some games have a move selection drop-down, and you can always manually type your move too. Helpful hints will appear above the move box as you enter your moves. One important feature to note is exploration. Before you submit your move, and while you're waiting for your opponent to move, you can make further moves to predict how the game might proceed and formulate your strategy.
play.movelist: Speaking of exploration, a list of all the moves made in the game is visible here. This will also include predicted future states you may have explored. When exploring, the current game state will have a box drawn around it. You can use the buttons above the move list to navigate. You can also use the arrow keys and the Home and End keys.
play.settings: And finally, open your user settings to change your profile, notification preferences, and exploration settings. You can disable these tours there as well.
play.status: In the status area you'll be told if any variants are active for this game as well as other game-specific data like scores or number of pieces in hand.
play.welcome: This is where the action happens! The play screen for every game is structured the same way. The name of the game will always appear here, front and centre, along with any descriptors like whether the game is part of a tournament.

Tournament.Description:
These are recurring tournaments for any game and variant combination. As long as there is enough interest, the next tournament starts automatically after the previous tournament ends. If you've joined the recurring series, then you will be automatically registered for the next tournament. If you "joined once" (an asterisk next to your name in the list of participants), then you will be removed after the next tournament starts.

After being requested, a tournament is open for registration for 2 weeks. If after the 2 week registration period there aren't at least 4 players registered, the tournament will stay open until the minimum number of players join. Otherwise the tournament starts, and the next tournament for the same game/variant combination is opened for registration. The next tournament starts a week after the current tournament ends.

Tournaments consist of divisions, with each division being a round-robin having at most 10 players. All games are played simultaneously. The time controls are: 36 hour increment, 72 hours starting time and 120 hours max time (hard time). Players are divided into divisions purely by their rating at the time the tournament starts. The highest rated players play in division 1, the next highest in division 2 and so on. Players are divided into divisions in such a way that all divisions have approximately the same number of players. First tiebreak is Sonneborn-Berger, that is, sum of defeated opponent scores. Second tiebreak is rating at the time the tournament started.

The site is completely free to join and play.

explanations.highestSingle: List of every recorded rating. The system ignores games explicitly flagged as unrated, and it ignores games that end before three moves have been made. The Elo rating starts at 1200 with a static *K* of 30. The Glicko rating uses the version 2 algorithm, the default starting values (initial rating 1500), and a rating period of sixty days (starting from the first day a particular game was recorded). Glicko ratings are presented as a 95% confidence range. The narrower that range, the more confident the system is in the rating. And finally, Trueskill is a rating system used by Microsoft in various online games. I used the default settings (rating range 0–50, starting at 25).
explanations.avgRatings: The average rating is just that: a straight average of all the Elo ratings recorded for that player. The weighted average is weighted by number of games played. For example, if you had a rating of 1300 in a game you played 10 times and 1200 in a game you only played twice, your average rating would be 1250, but your weighted average would be 1283.
explanations.topPlayers: This table lists each available game and variant combination along with the player with the highest Elo rating for that combination.
explanations.numPlays: This table lists each game, how many times it was played, by how many unique players, and the game's `h-index`. A game's h-index is the number of players who have played that game at least that many times (so an h-index of 5 means that 5 different players have played that game at least 5 times). It also provides a histogram of games completed for that game. The preview shows the last 10 weeks, with the most recent week on the right. Clicking on the preview will show you the full history of games completed, in seven-day "buckets," with the most recent week on the right.
explanations.playerStats: This shows each recorded player along with their total games played, a count of unique games, and the number of different opponents they played. It also provides an `h-index`, which represents the number of games you've played at least that many times (e.g., if you've played three different games only one time each, then your index is 1. As soon as you've played those three games at least three times *each*, the index will increase to 3). There's also an `h-index` for opponents you have faced. An activity histogram is also provided, showing the number of games completed each week, with the most recent week on the right. The preview shows the most recent ten weeks. Clicking on it will show you the full history.
explanations.gameStats: This table shows each game and variant combination along with the number of recorded games, the average length of the game (number of moves), the median length, the rate of first-player wins, and the draw rate (two-player games with more than two moves only). **The first-player win and draw stats should be treated with care!** The sample size is small and biased. There are many confounding factors that could explain an extreme rate. Note that the first-player win rate completely ignores whether the pie rule was invoked. Draws are counted as half a win for the first player when computing first-player win rate.
explanations.pieStats: Games that support the pie rule, showing how often the pie was invoked.
explanations.rivalryStats: Two-player pairings with at least fifty games together, ordered by games played. Pairs are anonymized until players opt in to be named.
explanations.tourneyStats: Shows each player who has participated in automated tournaments and their summary stats, including number of wins, number of top 50% finishes, and score. Your score is the sum of points received in each tournament. Points are awarded out of 100, based on your placement: first place gets 100 points, and last place gets none.

siteStats.hoursPerMoveIntro: Hours per move summarizes overall site pacing from completed games. Games ending by clock timeout, abandonment, or with fewer than two turns are excluded. Per-game rates are winsorized at the 2nd and 98th percentiles so extreme outliers do not dominate the summary. The mean is weighted by move count; the median treats each qualifying game equally. The trend chart shows the median hours per move for games completed each week (partial current week omitted).

dev.debugIntro: If there's a problem with your game, a developer may ask you to come to this page and send them the current game state. You can either click the "Copy" link below to copy the text to your clipboard and then paste it somewhere, or you can click the "Download" button to save a text file to your computer, which you can then send to the developers. Thank you!
dev.copyRendererJsonHelp: Renderer input for the board view currently shown (for Customize or debugging).
dev.injectNonDevWarning: If you are seeing this and are not a developer, please let an admin know immediately.
dev.injectDestructiveWarning: This is a destructive function. Pasting code here will obliterate the existing game state and cannot be undone. You have been warned.
dev.customCssWarning1: It is possible to customize the CSS of all instances of this particular game. <1>This is not something to do lightly!</1> Do not inject code you either do not understand or have not had vetted by someone you trust. Abstract Play and its developers are not responsible for any mishaps that may occur while using this feature.
dev.customCssWarning2: If you are certain you wish to continue, paste the CSS code below and click Save. If everything blows up, open the developer console and clear the local storage key <1>custom-css</1>, and that should reset everything. See the wiki for documentation, and join us on Discord to discuss.

customize.title: Customize Settings for {{gameName}}
customize.addColourHelp: Select a colour and click the "Add Colour" button. The default colours can be selected by clicking on the swatch. If the palette is empty, the default palette will be used.

background.label: Background
background.help: The colour of the area surrounding the board.

board.label: Board
board.help: The colour of the board itself. Defaults to background colour if not set.

strokes.label: Strokes
strokes.help: The colour of lines drawn on the board.

borders.label: Borders
borders.help: The colour of fixed piece borders.

fill.label: Fill
fill.help: The colour used to fill certain board elements. Basically, the "opposite" of the background.

customize.pasteSettingsHelp: Paste settings JSON here to apply.

lab.intro: A local play area for experimenting with games. Nothing here touches the server — positions and saved games live in your browser only.
lab.introLoggedIn: Experiment with games in the Playground. Saved positions sync to your account; your current session is also kept on this device so you can resume after a refresh.
lab.noSimultaneous: Playground supports sequential games only. Simultaneous games are not available.
lab.pasteHelp: Paste a serialized state from a live game debug dump, a Playground game export, or elsewhere. The game type is read from the state automatically. Simultaneous games are not supported.
lab.importLocalBanner: You have {{count}} Playground save(s) on this device. Copy them to your account?
lab.importLocalPartial: Some saves could not be copied: {{names}}
